query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature conditions, the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by inhibited atomic diffusion at grain boundaries and passivated surfaces, rather than by intrinsic chemical ordering. That is, modifying the nanoscale interfaces (via passivation or controlled annealing) will reduce atomic mobility at the interfaces, thereby preserving the alloy’s overall stability.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoalloys synthesized with a metastable nanoscale structure exhibiting unmodified (pristine) grain boundaries and surfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface passivation or controlled annealing treatment designed to modify the grain boundary chemistry and surface structure without altering the bulk composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature operating conditions (below the melting point but sufficiently high to activate diffusion processes) with two sets of nanoalloys—one set with modified surface/grain boundary characteristics and one control with unmodified interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary and surface characteristics that influence the rate of atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The treatment reduces the number and efficacy of fast diffusion pathways at the grain boundaries and surfaces, leading to sluggish atomic diffusion. This inhibited diffusion preserves the original nanoscale structure and minimizes chemical segregation and phase transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated control, the passivated/annealed nanoalloys will exhibit significantly lower atomic diffusion rates, maintain their initial phase morphology, and show reduced chemical inhomogeneities after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys with unmodified grain boundaries and surfaces that allow more rapid atomic diffusion, leading to observable chemical segregation or structural changes under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds for nanoalloys with identical bulk compositions where surface/interface treatments can effectively alter diffusion pathways; the temperatures must be high enough to activate diffusion processes yet below thresholds for melting or new phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of surface/passivation-induced sluggish diffusion versus any concurrent intrinsic chemical ordering effects remains partially uncertain and may vary with specific alloy systems and treatment parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples with identical bulk compositions. One set is subjected to a surface passivation/controlled annealing treatment to modify grain boundary and surface features, while the other set is left untreated. Both sets are then exposed to a defined high-temperature environment for a controlled period.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of atomic diffusion rates (e.g., using tracer diffusion techniques or atom probe tomography)
Assessment of nanoscale structural integrity via high-resolution electron microscopy
Chemical homogeneity analysis using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or similar methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated/annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in atomic diffusion rates, or if their structural and chemical stability is comparable to the untreated control, then the hypothesized dominance of interface-controlled, sluggish diffusion as the stability mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Diffusion involving atom transport from one location to another governs many important processes and behaviors such as precipitation and phase nucleation. The inherent chemical complexity in compositionally complex materials poses challenges for modeling atomic diffusion and the resulting formation of chemically ordered structures. Here, we introduce a neural network kinetics (NNK) scheme that predicts and simulates diffusion-induced chemical and structural evolution in complex concentrated chemical environments. The framework is grounded on efficient on-lattice structure and chemistry representation combined with artificial neural networks, enabling precise prediction of all path-dependent migration barriers and individual atom jumps. To demonstrate the method, we study the temperature-dependent local chemical ordering in a refractory NbMoTa alloy and reveal a critical temperature at which the B2 order reaches a maximum. The atomic jump randomness map exhibits the highest diffusion heterogeneity (multiplicity) in the vicinity of this characteristic temperature, which is closely related to chemical ordering and B2 structure formation. AbstractElastic stability is the basis for understanding structural responses to external stimuli in crystalline solids, including melting, incipient plasticity and fracture. In this work, elastic stability is investigated in a series of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) using in situ mechanical tests and atomic-resolution characterization in transmission electron microscopy. Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%. Such elastic strain-induced amorphization stands in intrinsic contrast to previously reported dislocation-mediated elastic instability and defect accumulation-mediated amorphization, introducing a form of elastic instability. Together with the first principle calculations and atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identify that the elastic strain-induced amorphization is closely related to the depressed dislocation nucleation due to the local atomic environment inhomogeneity of HEAs. Our findings provide insights for the understanding of the fundamental nature of physical mechanical phenomena like elastic instability and incipient plasticity.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical proper

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. frame.system: High-entropy nanoalloys synthesized with multiple principal elements, initially in a nanoscale, metastable state that becomes exposed to high-temperature environments.
frame.goal: To understand and define the dominant mechanisms governing both the structural integrity and chemical stability of these nanoalloys under high-temperature conditions.
frame.limitation: The precise mechanistic origin of the observed high-temperature stability is not well established; the interplay between kinetic effects (like sluggish diffusion), lattice distortions, and possible chemical ordering or segregation remains ambiguous.

decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy systems began by using atomistic simulations to reproduce nanoscale clustering and ordering phenomena (PMC4976365), which hinted at a link between local chemical rearrangements and mechanical responses. Subsequent studies tackled diffusion‐ and ordering‐related phenomena using advanced computational techniques (PMC11082203) and in situ atomic‐resolution observations (PMC11139900), gradually moving from indirect evidence from bulk or simulated behavior toward probing the dynamic evolution of defect structures and chemical inhomogeneities under applied loads or thermal stimuli. This trend illustrates efforts to discern how sluggish diffusion, local lattice distortions, and emergent chemical segregation together affect structural stability, yet these studies have not yet definitively isolated which factor is dominant in the nanoscale, high-temperature regime.
decision.unsolved: The precise mechanistic origin underlying the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of nanoalloys remains ambiguous – it is unclear whether sluggish diffusion within the metastable nanoscale structure, chemical ordering / segregation at surfaces or grain boundaries, or lattice distortion (or a combination thereof) is the principal contributor. Experimentally isolating these contributions under high-temperature conditions remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the nanoscale features – for example, by preparing high-entropy nanoalloys with identical bulk compositions but intentionally modified grain boundary characteristics and surface chemistries (e.g., via passivation layers or controlled annealing) to modulate diffusion and segregation rates.
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend from simulation and in situ characterization that identified competing roles for sluggish diffusion and chemical ordering. A controlled experiment that isolates the effect of surface and grain boundary treatments will distinguish whether the stability is primarily governed by inhibited atomic diffusion (supporting the sluggish diffusion hypothesis) or by driven chemical segregation/ordering at defects, thereby addressing the core gap observed in prior studies.
